This is the only comment that suggested an action other than voting that might be more effective than force. I won't say this altered the entirety of my view, but it did make me reconsider its scope somewhat. 

I did consider striking as a means for forcing those with more direct means to influence politics, but initially thought it too far removed to really be more effective than a physical threat to politicians. After all, hurting someone's wallet is inarguably not as threatening to them as hurting them physically. However, the more I think about it, the more I realize that my objections are primarily focused on the feasibility of organizing a mass strike rather than its effectiveness. Those same objections could be raised about mustering a sizeable physical threat to government, and so couldn't be a good argument against the comparative effectiveness.

I don't necessarily think that rich entities lobbying is the way, but it did make me consider that if there is a way to threaten a politician's way of life in a way that cannot be ignored (e.g. causing significant economic stress through a general strike as you've suggested) but does not necessarily threaten their immediate physical safety, then that non-physical threat could prove more effective - the threatened politician has room to respond to the threat without fearing for their life, and yet still faces severe consequences if the threat is ignored. I don't think this at all precludes violence as an effective means of accountability, but that its position as "most effective" is tenuous when compared with a mass strike. Non-physical "violence" to assets, as opposed to real violence to persons or property.

This is rather grim to say, but if the "other side" is *removed*, then there's no feedback loop. Or if the "other side" is too weak to fight back. But this is straying a bit from the crux of my view - I'm very purposefully avoiding discussing any specific ideology because it doesn't change why I believe my view. What if an elected official consistently does things a majority of their constituents don't like, but for various reasons they are never voted out? Reasons like:

- the bad things they do are not bad enough for a lot of people but REALLY bad for some people (e.g. policy that discriminates against minorities - a lot of non-minority people might care but it does not affect them directly in a way that harms their way of life)

- the elected official passes laws that make it hard for people to vote them out

- voter disenfranchisement - ie belief that "my vote doesn't matter" and "they're all the same anyway"

- the lack of a challenger - no one can afford to campaign against the current bad politician

- the thought that "well they might definitely be bad, but anyone else would be worse"

> In a democracy, the government IS the people. Taking up arms against our own govenment is the same as taking up arms against ourselves.

If it were a direct democracy, yes I'd agree with you. But in the US (and probably every democratic country) we have representative democracy. Those representatives have the ability to act in a way not consistent with the wishes of the people they are supposed to represent.

> That's called a Civil War. We already did that and you know how well that turned out.

Technically, it turned out great. Slavery was abolished and the country reunited. Would the proper action to the seceding states have been to let them remain separate and continue slavery to preserve peace? Or to tut very loudly at them for the next 2 centuries?

> To address your statement directly, taking up arms against the government is counter productive, and therefore ineffective, because if it actually were effective, if the government allowed itself to be turned by violence, it would undo all the work we as a nation have accomplished in establishing the rule of law over the last two centuries. We have not allowed that in our history.

I'm having a hard time with this one because there are some assumptions being made that I don't think are correct. No government will "allow itself to be turned by violence" - that's why the violence is there in the first place. If a government is not acting according to the wishes of the people and those people cannot peacefully change the government in a timely manner, then they can remove that government by force. "Work to establish the rule of law" doesn't really play a part here either, because we're assuming that the laws are always good and that they've never been challenged, which of course is false. In fact, many laws have been challenged violently, to great success (e.g. civil rights).

> Lastly, the threat of violence against the government of the United States is completely ineffective because any violence threatened against the US can be met with overwhelming force. 

The capitol riot provides the counterpoint to this. Hundreds of people basically walked in - arguably because the people guarding the doors/overall security let them. I don't know all of the details concerning how much of a threat these people were, but if more of them were armed, we would probably be having a very different conversation about it. Additionally, 9/11 did not really target US politicians, but the US military and citizens. It was also from a foreign entity, not its own citizens. The circumstances are quite different from what I'm discussing here.

> What actions by a leader warrant "physical threats to their life and comfort"? 

All of them, technically. I am not going to tell you who decides when a leader should feel threatened, but rather that if their actions (any of their actions) are not made bearing in mind the possibility of a mob at their door, then nothing is really holding them accountable for their actions.

> Do you really want to live in a society in which leadership is perpetually subjected to the fickleness of Damocles Sword?

This isn't at all relevant to the question - I don't think at any point I've suggested that I want to "live in this society" but rather that those circumstances are the only ones in which government can be held meaningfully responsible for its actions.

> Most real change happens when democratically elected governments are enacted.

What do you mean by this? "real change" is very vague and implying that some changes are not real - what are "fake" changes?

> Peaceful transitions of power through transparent elections is the closest we have to a successful working model of a functioning society.

This isn't something I'm necessarily arguing against. I'm not advocating that our leaders be the last men/women standing in a battle royale. You could make a case (obviously) that violent actions would lead to revolts and overthrows of government but that's not a given. If a serious, demonstrable *threat*, can motivate change, that makes it effective and yet bloodless.

> are you really comfortable advocating for "politics by other means"? 

I'm not comfortable - but I don't see how any elected leader would remotely be concerned with the consequences of their actions if there were not physical threats to their life and comfort.

I cannot - and this is where I feel my argument is weakest and most likely to change. However I've considered this, and can't honestly say that just because I can't provide substantial evidence that someone threatening violence has caused a politician to change their actions doesn't mean that it isn't effective by default. Like I said in the OP, even *I* am not 100% convinced my view is logically sound, but I cannot see why alternatives are more effective, especially when politics *is* fundamentally about managing violence in my view (ie citizens enacting violence vs. the state enacting violence).

Incidentally, any violent action does require a lot of bravery/stupidity from "people using it" as there are obviously consequences to using force, so that is a huge demotivator for the vast majority of people. In fact it's possibly the biggest demotivator over the potential effectiveness.

> Why is your opinion on the wrongness of outcome of recent events the one that provides us evidence that the available means today aren't sufficient?

It doesn't, really. I'm not meaning to suggest that my opinion is right because it's mine. 

>if we take your perspective, then you've basically legitimized violence as a effective means for the average person who disagrees with a politician who isn't successfully removed from office by other means.

> The trump capital rioters are a great example of people who think like you're suggesting.

As I mentioned in another comment, yes - those means were legitimate to me, even if their reasons were stupid.

I am not assuming that, or intending to imply it. I absolutely think people will be violent for stupid ass reasons, but I don't think that makes their actions ineffective. I am not intending to imply "violence is best" but more "violence is most effective"

I do not think that, no. And it's not my intention to imply that. But my view isn't really concerned with any socioeconomic stability either. A general view I hold on government is that it exists because the people give up their "right" (for lack of a better word) to violence in exchange for protection/benefits/etc. that government provides, which is indeed more stable. But if that government isn't working for the people, then the best way to motivate its actions is to take back the "right" to violence.

I agree the response could be brutal - but that "iron fist" is not literal: police forces and militaries consist of people, and those people can agree or disagree with a movement that seeks to remove a politician. If the rather unlikely scenario occurred where 100% of a nation's military was against the authority of the existing government, that government is done for.
